messages.subject: Controlling for L2 proficiency when its role may differ between stimuli
messages.subject_clean: Controlling for L2 proficiency when its role may differ between stimuli
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I’m trying my hand at preregistering the design and analysis of a 
project. It’s an instructive experience, but I’ve hit an obstacle where 
I can’t really decide up front as to what’s the best alternative.

Without going into too much detail, I want to investigate the degree to 
which two groups of L2 learners rely on their L1 when assigning 
grammatical gender to L2 nouns. Each participant will assign grammatical 
gender (masculine, feminine, neuter) to 21 stimuli whose cognates are 
either masculine or feminine in the L1. To simplify the analysis, the 
participants’ responses will be converted to ‘congruent’ (i.e. masculine 
response if L1 = masculine or feminine response if L1 = feminine) or 
‘incongruent’ (all other cases). I should then be able to see whether 
one group of learners show a higher tendency towards congruent responses.

It is possible, however, that one group of learners happens to know more 
about L2 gender than the other. Knowledge of L2 gender can impact both 
negatively or positively on the L2-L1 congruency effect, depending on 
the L2 and L1 gender of the stimuli. If the correct L2 gender and the L1 
gender are congruent (e.g. both masculine), those more knowledgeable 
about L2 gender assignments should be more likely to produce ‘congruent’ 
responses. If the correct L2 gender and the L1 gender are incongruent 
(e.g. neuter vs. masculine), those more knowledgeable about L2 gender 
assignments should be less likely to produce ‘congruent’ responses.

So how should I try to control for inter-group differences in L2 
knowledge as far as possible? I will have at my disposal participants’ 
L2 gender assignments on 15 filler items and could distill an ‘L2 gender 
knowledge’ index from those responses (number of correct responses). I 
can think of three possibilities of how to use this:

1. Split up the sample according the participants’ L2 gender knowledge 
(e.g. in four parts) and conduct separate analyses on each subsample. I 
wouldn’t be too happy about this, though, as I wouldn’t know how to 
combine these different subset analyses.

2. Include ‘L2 gender knowledge’ (i.e. score on filler items) and 
‘congruency of correct L2 gender and L1 gender’ as well as an 
interaction between them into the model as fixed-effect control 
predictors. ‘L2 gender knowledge’ should have a positive effect on 
‘response congruency’ if the correct L2 gender and the L1 gender are 
congruent and a negative effect if they’re incongruent. But in this case 
it’s possible that the absolute effect of L2 gender knowledge differs 
between congruent and incongruent stimuli, and I’m not sure that’s 
really what I’d want.

3. Multiply ‘L2 gender knowledge’ by -1 if the correct L2 gender and the 
L1 gender are incongruent, and use it as a fixed-effect control 
predictor (and perhaps also as a by-stimulus random slope). In this case 
L2 gender knowledge will have the same effect for congruent and 
incongruent stimuli, but its meaning will differ.

At the moment I’m leaning towards the third option, but perhaps someone 
sees a problem with that or has better ideas.

Thanks for any feedback,

Jan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jan,

to me option number 2 is the most conceptually appealing. I don't see the
downside of that option. If the effect of L2 knowledge is asymmetric for
congruent and incongruent stimuli, then that's how it is empirically (which
could have a variety of interpretations, since presumably there will be
many additional differences between these stimuli that could plausibly
explain the difference in the effects size of L2 knowledge).

Of course, all of this assumes that the measure of L2 knowledge that you
obtain from fillers is sufficiently independent of the congruency
manipulation? I don't understand enough of your experiment to see how this
could be the case (i.e., how the fillers could be neither congruent nor
incongruent). If the independence assumption is not (sufficiently)
warranted, any of the approaches risks being circular.

In any case, I don't like option 1. It reduces but does not eliminate the
problem (admittedly the other options aren't not guaranteed to eliminate
the problem either, but at least they do so modulo a) the independence
assumption described above, b) measurement noise in the L2 knowledge, and
c) any linearity assumption you'd be applying to the effect of L2
knowledge).

Flo

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jan,

I'll add a vote for some version of option 2 (and agree that option 1 is
probably the worst).  But I guess like Florian I'm also curious about why
you think responses to fillers would provide a good index of "L2 gender
knowledge".  Are they non-cognates?  Are the words (targets or fillers)
likely to be words that the participants already know?  L1-L2 transfer can
get pretty complex (i.e., non-linear) when you look at proficiency vs.
cognates.  For example, very early on, L2 speakers may transfer a lot, but
then as they acquire more counter-examples they may get over-cautious, and
unwilling to assume that gender transfers at all, and then as they acquire
more proficiency, they get more accurate.  And these patterns can be
different for cognates vs. non-cognates.

I think if I were in your shoes, I'd consider trying to get an independent
measure of L2 proficiency, something like a simple cloze test or other
vocab-based measure, as a general index of "how likely are they to know any
given word's gender".  I'd also consider including lexical frequency as an
additional (item-level) covariate, since more common words may be more
likely to be known at a given proficiency level.  Maybe this isn't a big
concern given your materials, but maybe something worth considering.
Anyway, use some independent vocab-based index of proficiency as your
interaction effect under option 2.  But you may also want to pre-register
some non-linear interactions (e.g., something u-shaped like high congruency
effects for low- and high-proficiency, lower congruency effect for
mid-proficiency), though this might again depend on the actual levels of L2
proficiency in your sample.  So, maybe a quadratic or even cubic regression
term.  On the other hand, this may be getting way too complex for the data
you intend to collect, so you might want to just pre-register a simple
linear interaction, and then just plan to look at some polynomial or other
non-linear stuff as an exploratory analysis.

my two cents,
-scott

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Thanks for your comments. I see that some more details that are didn’t 
include for fear of blowing up the opening post are in order.

The gender system of the L1 is as follows. In the written standard and 
the Northern part of the language area, only two genders exist: common 
and neuter. In Southern substandard varieties, a three-way distinction 
exists: masculine, feminine and neuter. For all intents and purposes, 
standard neuter maps perfectly onto substandard neuter. The L2, like the 
Southern substandard, has a three-gender system, and I wondered whether 
Southerners, who are literate and were schooled in the two-gender 
standard, make use of their three-gender system when assigning gender in 
the L2.

I have a list of standard common-gender nouns which I know to be 
predominantly masculine or feminine in the substandard. The RQ is 
whether Southern participants assign L2 gender to stimuli whose standard 
cognates are common-gender on the basis of the substandard gender; the 
standard doesn’t provide clues as to how to distinguish masculine from 
feminine gender here. In reality, the correct L2 gender (masc., fem., 
neuter) for these nouns cuts across the L1 gender categories – at least 
in this experiment –, but it proved impossible to fully balance them 
(simply not enough stimuli available for all cells).

By my reckoning, I could code the participants’ responses to stimuli 
with a common-gender standard cognate for substandard congruency: 
congruent if they assign masculine gender and the substandard gender is 
masculine or if they assign feminine gender and the substandard gender 
is feminine, incongruent in other cases. In this case, transfer from the 
substandard is a likely explanation if Southern tend to provide more 
congruent responses. (An alternative would be to code the participants’ 
responses for their correctness and add substandard L1 gender as a 
predictor; Southerners should then be sensitive to this predictor to a 
greater degree than Northerners. That is, I’d need an interaction 
between Region and substandard gender. But I think the two approaches 
accomplish the same thing, and fewer terms would be needed if I code for 
congruency rather than correctness. A less satisfying alternative would 
be to forget about the North and just model the Southerners’ responses 
and include substandard gender as a predictor. But such an effect may be 
driven by formal or semantic stimulus-related characteristics; I need 
the Northerners as a control group.)

But I’ve been thinking that an alternative or additional explanation for 
a larger congruency effect for Southerners (or a Region*substandard 
gender interaction) might be that (a) something about the stimuli (all 
monomorphemic, monosyllabic and inanimate) nonetheless says ‘masculine’ 
or ‘feminine’ to Northerners and Southerners alike, too, along the same 
lines as the Southern substandard distinction but (b) Northerners know 
more about L2 and therefore ignore point (a). To rule this latter 
explanation out as best I might, some measure of the participants’ L2 
knowledge seemed useful.

The task also contains 15 L2 stimuli whose L1 cognates are neuter in 
both the standard and the substandard. For five of these stimuli, the L2 
gender is neuter, for six it is masculine, for four it is feminine 
(inanimate feminine L2 words with neuter L1 cognates are few and far 
between, unfortunately). These are all fairly transparent cognates, so I 
presume that most participants will ‘know’ these words receptively. My 
reasoning was that participants with little to no L2 knowledge will 
essentially pursue one of these three strategies: (a) random guessing; 
(b) tick neuter everywhere (transfer); (c) tick another response 
everywhere (e.g. masculinisation strategy). Either strategy should 
result in a fairly low score compared to participants with more 
extensive L2 knowledge. True, strategy (b) would be transfer-based, but 
not uniquely substandard-based (the strategy is available to both 
Northerners and Southerners).

@Florian: Does that seem reasonable?

I do have an alternative, but less direct L2 proficiency measure at my 
disposal: self-assessments on a CEFR-based scale. I guess a cloze test 
or a vocabulary task with non-cognates may be alternatives, but these, 
too, are indirect. The test will be run online, so I’m doing all I can 
not to scare away customers mid-task. (I’ve considered including 
non-cognates in the gender assignment task, but low-level participants 
seem to have a knack for seeing cognate relationships were there are 
none, especially if many cognates occur elsewhere in the task, so what I 
intend as non-cognates may not be non-cognates to the participants.) The 
suggestions about non-linear proficiency effects and word frequency are 
excellent, but seeing as writing up the analysis without the data at 
hand is proving difficult enough as it is, I went with Scott’s 
suggestion and reserved those for an exploratory analysis. (I guess one 
could also imagine that early on, learners aren’t particularly keen on 
transferring L1 gender to the L2 but grow more fond of it when acquiring 
more and more positive examples.)

Oh, and one more thing - said Columbo:

“If the effect of L2 knowledge is asymmetric for congruent and 
incongruent stimuli, then that's how it is empirically (which could have 
a variety of interpretations, since presumably there will be many 
additional differences between these stimuli that could plausibly 
explain the difference in the effects size of L2 knowledge).”

I understand what you mean, Florian, but wouldn’t you also be able to 
account for such ‘many additional differences’ by forcing the model to 
produce one fixed parameter estimate for ‘effect of L2 knowledge on 
response congruency’ but allowing this effect to vary between stimuli 
(random slope)? Whatever many additional differences exist, they’re 
unlikely to precisely follow the masculine/feminine distinction in the 
substandard?

Thanks a lot for your contributions, Scott, Florian and (privately) Dan!

I agree. More generally, you want to control for response biases. To me
this would be the starting point:

L2 gender guess == masculine ~ I(L1 Southern gender == masculine) * I(L2
gender == masculine) * (L1 variety of speaker == southern) + (1 + I(L1
Southern gender == masculine) * I(L2 gender == masculine) | participant) +
(1 + I(L1 variety of speaker == southern) | word)

This rules out biases based on the word, overall response biases, etc. It
is conservative and might not converge depending on how much data you have.
You'd be predicting

   - a main effect of L2 gender (e.g., capturing the idea that participants
   might have SOME knowledge about L2)
   - an interaction between L1 southern gender and L1 variety of the
   speaker (if the answer to your RG is affirmative)
   - potentially an interaction between L2 gender and L1 variety (if
   northerners indeed know more about L2, as you hypothesize below).
   - There might be additional biases that come out as e.g., a 3-way
   interaction.

You could simplify this model to remove the 3-way, but if you can afford it
(as simulations can test), I wouldn't since the above is your full design.
Slightly better would be simplifications in the random effect structure. in
particular, you could remove that L2 gender == masculine by-subject slope
(and with it the interaction), if removing random correlations isn't
sufficient.

I realize that this model is more complex what you suggested but coding
correct or congruent without including the full factorial *does* make some
assumptions (and especially since your design isn't balanced with regard to
L2 gender, these assumptions could get tricky, though perhaps you've
thought through them).

messages.subject: Re: Correlation from extreme values
messages.body_plain:
With regard to interpretation: This is an example of the „Simpsons’s paradox“ (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpson%27s_paradox<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpson's_paradox>)

While there appears to be a strong correlation between x and y, the data rather suggest that there is an underlying dichotomous grouping factor that better explains the pattern. If you control for this grouping factor, for example, in a linear regression model, the apparent correlation between x and y disappears (or, as in some of the Simpson's paradox examples, it can even reverse).

Code to confirm this:

Xaxis=c(1,3,3,5,6,8,85,87,90,92,97,98)
Yaxis=c(2,10,8,4,12,2,85,80,94,82,80,87)
Data = data.frame(Xaxis,Yaxis)

# create grouping factor
Data$group <- factor(rep(c("A","B"), each = 6))

# simple regression
mod1 <- lm(Yaxis ~ Xaxis, data = Data)
summary(mod1)

# multiple regression controlling for group
mod2 <- lm(Yaxis ~ Xaxis + group, data = Data) # Xaxis is now clearly n.s.
summary(mod2)

messages.subject: Re: Correlation from extreme values
messages.body_plain:
Hello Ben,


An additional thing you may want to consider is that extreme-group sampling can lead to systematically larger effect sizes than ordinary sampling:


---

library(MASS)

sim.cors <- function(n = 100) {
dat <- mvrnorm(n, Sigma = matrix(c(1, 0.8, 0.8, 1), 2), mu = c(0, 0))
cor.tot <- cor(dat)[1, 2]
cor.reduced <- cor(dat[rank(dat[,1]) <= 10 | rank(dat[,1]) >= 91, ])[1, 2]
return(list(cor.tot, cor.reduced))
}

cors <- replicate(1e3, sim.cors())

plot(unlist(cors[1, ]), unlist(cors[2, ]),
     xlim = c(0.6, 1), ylim = c(0.6, 1),
     xlab = "correlation full range",
     ylab = "correlation extreme cases")
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lwd = 2, col = "blue")

---


I.e., for the same bivariate relationship, you'll end up with larger correlation coefficients if you've sampled at the extremes (largest and lowest values) than if you were indiscriminate in your choice of x-values. This may be important if you want to use the correlation coefficient to communicate the strength of the bivariate relationship.


Regression coefficients don't show this effect (from an earlier simulation<http://janhove.github.io/reporting/2015/02/05/standardised-vs-unstandardised-es> I ran):


[center]


Cheers,

Jan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Just another perspective on what everyone else is saying: just think
carefully about why your distributions look like they are.  That is, each
variable is extremely bimodal.  Why?  If it's an artifact of how you
sampled, then Jan's point is especially relevant.  If there is some
underlying categorical structure, like classes of "high" and "low" values
for both variables, then you probably just want something like a
contingency table, and the variation around each class "cloud" could just
be a type of measurement error.  So maybe a simple correlation isn't
necessarily going to give you the "wrong" inference, but it's missing
something potentially very important about how your data is structured.

-scott

messages.subject: Validating and testing generalisability of regression model that is the result of data exploration
messages.subject_clean: Validating and testing generalisability of regression model that is the result of data exploration
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I’d like to bounce an idea for an upcoming data analysis off you.

Context/goal: My colleagues have a pretty substantial number (I don’t 
know the precise number yet, but let's assume about 800) of short 
written productions in three languages. The texts were written by 
monolingual and bilingual children, who wrote two texts in each of their 
languages (i.e. two texts for monolinguals, four texts for bilinguals) 
at three points in time (i.e. 6 texts in total for monolinguals, 12 
texts in total for bilinguals). At each point in time, the children were 
given the same two topics to write about; bilinguals wrote about the 
same topic twice each time.

Human raters will be asked to rate the lexical diversity of these texts, 
and the idea is to see which combination of algorithmic lexical 
diversity measures that have been proposed in the literature best 
captures these human ratings. Ideally, the findings could also be used 
to suggest a combination of relatively easy-to-compute algorithmic 
measures and their weighting to educators and researchers interested in 
lexical diversity in bi- and monolingual children who don’t have the 
time or resources to collect human ratings.

In essence, the two questions guiding the analysis are:

(1) Which combination of algorithmic measures best predicts human 
lexical diversity ratings?

(2) How well does this combination predict human lexical diversity ratings?

We’ll have a substantial number of collinear algorithmic measures at our 
disposal, and I want to avoid the situation where we end up with a model 
with a spectacularly good fit to the data but with no chance of 
predicting human ratings for similar but new texts. Here’s the course of 
action I’d like to propose to my colleagues - but perhaps you have 
better suggestions.

 1.

    For each written production, compute the mean human rating.

 2.

    Divide the data into a training, a validation and a test set by
    first blocking on the time of data collection (T1, T2, T3), the
    topic of the writing task (Topic A, Topic B), language (French,
    German, Portuguese) and participant group (monolingual, bilingual)
    and, within each block, picking 50% of the texts at random for the
    training set, 25% for the validation set and 25% for the test set.

 3.

    Explore the training set and build a number of theoretically
    plausible and reasonably well fitting multiple regression models
    (incl. transformations and rules for outlier treatment).

 4.

    Apply these regression models to the validation set (same
    predictors, same parameters) and select the best-fitting model.

 5.

    Apply this best-fitting model to the test set to estimate the
    model’s chances of predicting human ratings for unseen texts.

Does anyone see any problems with this approach? E.g. problems related 
to the dependencies in the data (multiple ratings per text, multiple 
ratings per rater, multiple productions per child)? If so, any 
suggestions of how these could be solved? Thanks!

Hi everyone

Thanks for your all your help! I probably should have given a bit more information at the start: These particular data are made up but represent the proportion of past vs present-tense forms in (X axis) an input corpus and (Y axis) an elicited production study. We deliberately chose highly past-biased or present-biased verbs (though I’m now wondering if this was a mistake).

The impression I’m getting from the replies so far is that this is probably OK - and that the effect we get is meaningful - though its size will have been inflated by our choice of highly biased verbs.

We are now planning a follow-up study and would be interested to hear people’s views on whether we should again choose highly biased verbs (to make it more likely that we will detect an effect if there is one to be found) or sample evenly across the distribution (to get a more realistic estimate of the size of any effect - not that this is particularly important for our purposes).

Thanks
Ben

messages.subject: Re: Correlation from extreme values
messages.body_plain:
Daniel,

I think this is an instance of the well-known problem of "restriction of
range", which can reduce correlation coefficients (a popular correction
is known as Thorndike Case 2 and is implemented in rangeCorrection() in
the "psych" package).

But isn't this different from the effect that Vanhove pointed out?

As an aside, it appears that restricted ranges can also *increase*
correlations in some circumstances (Wiseman, 1967; Zimmerman and
Williams, 2000).

João


Wiseman, S. (1967). The effect of restriction of range upon correlation
coefficients. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 37, 248–252.
http://10.1111/j.2044-8279.1967.tb01933.x

Zimmerman, D. W., & Williams, R. H. (2000). Restriction of range and
correlation in outlier-prone distributions. Applied Psychological
Measurement, 24, 267–280. http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/01466210022031741

messages.subject: Re: Correlation from extreme values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

On 22.03.2016 21:39, Daniel Ezra Johnson wrote:
> I noticed in the earlier discussion an implication that by sampling 
> towards the extremes of a distribution, the correlation is somehow 
> inflated. I wouldn't say that -- it's larger, but it's probably 
> usually more accurate to say that by sampling only in the middle of a 
> distribution, the correlation is deflated. At least that's what I 
> learned from File:Correlation_range_dependence.svg 
> <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Correlation_range_dependence.svg> ?

Both, actually. The true population correlation for this bivariate 
relationship is 0.8. By sampling randomly, you end up with an unbiased 
estimate; by sampling at the extremes, you end up with an 
overestimation; by sampling in the middle, you end up with an 
underestimation.

---
library(MASS)

sim.cors <- function(n = 100) {
   dat <- mvrnorm(n, Sigma = matrix(c(1, 0.8, 0.8, 1), 2), mu = c(0, 0))
   cor.tot <- cor(dat)[1, 2]
   cor.extreme <- cor(dat[rank(dat[,1]) <= 10 | rank(dat[,1]) >= 91, 
])[1, 2]
   cor.middle <- cor(dat[rank(dat[,1]) >= 40 & rank(dat[,1]) < 60, ])[1, 2]
   return(list(cor.tot, cor.extreme, cor.middle))
}

cors <- replicate(1e3, sim.cors())

plot(unlist(cors[1, ]), unlist(cors[2, ]),
      xlim = c(0.6, 1), ylim = c(0.6, 1),
      xlab = "correlation full range",
      ylab = "correlation extreme cases")
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lwd = 2, col = "blue")
summary(unlist(cors[1, ])) # full range
#Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
  #0.6319  0.7774  0.8031  0.7996  0.8264  0.8889
summary(unlist(cors[2, ])) # extreme cases
# Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
# 0.7957  0.9119  0.9328  0.9278  0.9473  0.9821

plot(unlist(cors[1, ]), unlist(cors[3, ]),
      xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1),
      xlab = "correlation full range",
      ylab = "correlation middle cases")
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lwd = 2, col = "blue")
summary(unlist(cors[3, ])) # middle cases
#   Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max.
# -0.49170  0.03827  0.20250  0.19600  0.35560  0.78330
---
